title: API Fundamentals
subtitle: Read, test and document real API calls safely, and scope API integrations a business can rely on.
description: Learn how apps exchange data through HTTP requests and JSON responses, using free tools on your phone or laptop. You will practise on open APIs, test a payment API safely in test mode, handle errors, paging and webhooks, and finish with a documented exploration, an integration spec and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Break any API request into method, URL, headers and body, and read the status code and JSON response
Send GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests with Hoppscotch or Postman against practice APIs
Authenticate with a Bearer key in test mode and store keys so leaks are unlikely and quickly contained
Handle rate limits, paged lists and signed webhooks, and verify payments before acting on them
Run discovery, write a one-page integration spec and price it with clear scope
Produce a documented API exploration and a 90-day plan for your portfolio
audience: Women who already work with digital tools, such as virtual assistants, no-code builders, automation learners and project coordinators, and want to understand and test APIs properly.
tools: Smartphone or laptop with a modern browser
Free practice APIs: Open-Meteo and JSONPlaceholder
Optional: a Paystack account in test mode

modules.title: How Apps Talk: Requests, HTTP and JSON
modules.overview: You will learn what an API is, make real requests from your phone, and read the HTTP methods, status codes, headers and JSON that every API uses. By the end you can look at a raw request and response and explain exactly what happened.

lessons.title: What an API really is: the request and response conversation
objectives: Explain in plain words what an API is and who the client and the server are
Break any API URL into scheme, host, path and query parameters
Make your first real API request from a phone browser and recognise the reply
Tell the difference between a web page meant for people and an API response meant for programs

blocks.text: An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a published set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data or for an action. A weather app on your phone does not measure the weather itself. It sends a message to a weather service, and the service sends back numbers. The rules about how to ask, and what the answer will look like, are the API.

Every API conversation has two sides. The **client** is the program that asks: a mobile app, a website, a spreadsheet tool, or you typing into a testing tool. The **server** is the computer that answers. The question is called a **request** and the answer is called a **response**. Almost every modern web API uses **HTTP**, the same language your browser uses to load web pages, usually in its secure form, **HTTPS**.

blocks.name: data-transfer
blocks.alt: Two devices passing data back and forth
blocks.caption: An API call is a short conversation: the client sends a request and the server sends back a response.

blocks.text: A restaurant picture, then the real thing

Think of a buka. You do not walk into the kitchen. You tell the attendant what you want from the menu, the attendant takes it to the kitchen, and food comes back on a plate. The menu is like the **API documentation**: it lists what you can ask for. The attendant is the **API**. The kitchen is the server's private system, which you never see. If you order something that is not on the menu, you get a polite refusal, not a meal. APIs behave the same way: ask for something the documentation does not list and you get an error message.

blocks.title: One API call from start to finish
items: Client builds a request
Request travels over HTTPS
Server checks and processes
Server sends a response
Client reads the data
blocks.caption: Every API call, however large the system, follows this same five-step round trip.

blocks.text: Reading an API address

Each thing you can ask an API for has its own address, called an **endpoint**. An endpoint is written as a URL, and every part of the URL has a job. Take this real request to Open-Meteo, a free weather API that does not need a key for non-commercial use:
`https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=6.45&longitude=3.39&current=temperature_2m&timezone=Africa/Lagos`

head: Part
In this URL
What it does
rows: Says the conversation is encrypted HTTP
The server you are talking to
Which endpoint on that server; v1 is the version of the API
Extra settings, written as name=value pairs joined by &
The details of your question: where, what, and which clock to use

blocks.text: Notice that the question is in the URL itself. The latitude and longitude point to a spot in Lagos (approximately), `current=temperature_2m` asks for the current air temperature at 2 metres above ground, and `timezone=Africa/Lagos` asks the server to give times in Nigerian time instead of world time (UTC). Change the numbers and you are asking about a different place.

blocks.title: Worked example: your first API call from a phone
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a virtual assistant in Ibadan who keeps hearing developers mention APIs. She has a smartphone with Chrome and about 10 minutes.
steps: She opens Chrome and types the Open-Meteo URL above, but changes latitude to 7.38 and longitude to 3.94, which is approximately Ibadan.
Instead of a web page with pictures, the screen fills with text in curly brackets. That text is the response, written in a format called JSON.
She finds the word `current` and inside it `temperature_2m` followed by a number. That number is the current temperature in degrees Celsius.
She also sees `current_units`, which tells her the unit of each number, so she never has to guess whether a value is Celsius or Fahrenheit.
She changes `current=temperature_2m` to `current=temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m` and reloads. Now the response includes wind speed too, because she asked a bigger question.
blocks.result: Amaka has made two real API requests with no code and no account. She has seen that the URL carries the question and the JSON carries the answer. The exact numbers she sees will differ from anyone else's because the weather changes.

blocks.text: Web pages versus API responses

A normal web page is built for human eyes: fonts, colours, buttons. An API response is built for programs: plain structured text with no decoration. The same company often has both. Paystack, for example, has a dashboard that business owners click through, and an API at `https://api.paystack.co` that a website's code talks to. The dashboard and the API can show the same transaction, but only the API can be used automatically by another program.
Where you meet APIs every day

items: Paying for an order online: the shop's website asks a payment company's API to start a payment, and later asks it whether the payment succeeded.
Logging in with Google: the site asks Google's API to confirm who you are, so the site never sees your Google password.
Delivery tracking: the shop's system asks the courier's API for the latest status of your parcel.
Automation tools such as Zapier or Make: every app connection they offer is built on that app's API.

blocks.title: Advanced does not mean coding
blocks.text: This course is for people who want to understand and test APIs properly: virtual assistants, no-code builders, project coordinators and analysts. You will read raw requests and responses and use free testing tools. You will not need to write an app, but what you learn is exactly what developers use.

Finally, remember that an API is a promise. The company that publishes it promises that if you ask in the documented way, you will get an answer in the documented shape. Your job, as someone who works with APIs, is to read that promise carefully, ask correctly, and check that the answer really matches.

takeaways: An API is a published set of rules that lets one program request data or actions from another
The client sends a request; the server returns a response, usually over HTTPS
A URL has a scheme, host, path and query string, and each part has a job
API responses are structured text for programs, not decorated pages for people

activity.title: Make and label three API requests
steps: Open the Open-Meteo forecast URL from this lesson in your phone browser.
Change the latitude and longitude to your own town (look them up on a map app; approximate is fine).
Add `wind_speed_10m` to the `current` parameter, separated by a comma, and reload.
Copy the URL and write it on paper, then circle and label the scheme, host, path and each parameter.
Note down the temperature value and its unit from `current_units`.
activity.evidence: A photo of your labelled URL and a screenshot of the response showing the temperature and its unit

lessons.title: Speaking HTTP: methods, status codes and headers
objectives: Choose the correct HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) for a given task
Explain what safe and idempotent mean and why they matter for retries
Read a status code and say whether the problem is on the client side or the server side
Name the common headers and explain what Content-Type, Accept and Authorization do

blocks.text: Every HTTP request has three main parts: a **method** (the verb: what you want to do), a **target** (the endpoint URL), and **headers** (labelled notes about the request). Some requests also carry a **body**, which is the data you are sending. Every response comes back with a **status code** (a three-digit number that says how it went), its own headers, and usually a body.

blocks.name: server-status
blocks.alt: A person checking the status of servers
blocks.caption: Status codes are the server's first, short answer about how your request went.

blocks.text: The five methods you will use most

head: Method
What it means
Safe?
Idempotent?
Everyday example
rows: Send new data, usually creating something
Start a new payment; create a customer
Replace a whole item with what you send
Change only some fields of an item
Update just a customer's phone number

blocks.text: Two words in that table matter a lot. A **safe** method does not change anything on the server; it only reads. GET is safe, which is why you could test it in a browser in the last lesson without harming anything. An **idempotent** method gives the same end result whether you send it once or five times. Deleting the same item twice still leaves it deleted. Replacing a record with the same data twice still leaves the same record.

POST is neither safe nor idempotent. If you send the same "create payment" POST twice, you may create two payments. This is why, when a POST request seems to hang, you should not simply press send again. You first check whether the first one went through. Many payment APIs give you a unique **reference** for each transaction so you can look it up instead of guessing.
Status codes: the server's short answer
Status codes come in five families. You can tell a lot from the first digit alone:

items: **1xx informational**: rare in everyday API work.
**2xx success**: 200 OK (it worked), 201 Created (a new item was made, common after POST), 204 No Content (it worked and there is nothing to send back, common after DELETE).
**3xx redirection**: 301 Moved Permanently (the address has changed), 304 Not Modified (use your saved copy).

**4xx client error**: the problem is in your request. 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (you have not proved who you are), 403 Forbidden (the server knows who you are but you are not allowed), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Content, 429 Too Many Requests.
**5xx server error**: the problem is on their side. 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable.

blocks.title: 4xx or 5xx: whose problem is it?
items: 4xx: fix your request
5xx: their side failed
blocks.caption: The first digit of the status code tells you where to start looking.

blocks.text: A useful habit: **401 versus 403**. A 401 means the server did not receive valid proof of who you are, so check that your key is present and correctly typed. A 403 means the server accepted who you are but your account is not permitted to do this, so a different key will not help; you need different permissions.
Headers: the labels on the envelope
Headers are name and value pairs sent before the body. You will see these again and again:

items: `Content-Type: application/json` tells the server the body you are sending is JSON.
`Accept: application/json` tells the server you would like JSON back.
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` carries your proof of identity, such as an API secret key.
`Retry-After: 3600` (in a response) tells you how many seconds to wait before trying again, often sent with 429 or 503.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a raw request and response
blocks.context: For example, Funmi is helping a developer debug a weather feature on a Lagos events website. The developer shares the raw text of one request and its response.
steps: Request line: `GET /v1/forecast?latitude=6.45&longitude=3.39&current=temperature_2m HTTP/1.1`. Funmi notes the method is GET, so nothing on the server can be changed by it.
Request headers: `Host: api.open-meteo.com` and `Accept: application/json`. The host tells her which server; Accept says the client wants JSON.
Response line: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`. The first digit is 2, so the request succeeded.
Response header: `Content-Type: application/json`. The body is JSON, as asked.

A second log line shows `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` for a request where latitude was typed as `6,45` with a comma. The first digit is 4, so the fix is in the request: use a full stop as the decimal point.
blocks.result: Funmi traces the broken weather box on the website to one badly formatted number. No one needed to contact the weather provider, because the status code pointed to a client-side mistake.

blocks.title: Read the error body too
blocks.text: A status code is the headline; the response body is the story. Many APIs send a short JSON message with an error, for example a message saying which field is missing. Always read both before changing anything.

takeaways: GET reads; POST creates; PUT replaces; PATCH changes part; DELETE removes
Never blindly resend a POST: check first whether the first request succeeded
2xx means success, 4xx means fix your request, 5xx means the server side failed
401 means prove who you are; 403 means you are known but not allowed
Headers like Content-Type, Accept and Authorization carry the instructions around the data

activity.title: Build a status code card
steps: On one page or phone note, write the five status code families and what each first digit means.
Under 2xx and 4xx, write the specific codes from this lesson and one line each in your own words.
For each of these tasks, write the method you would use: read a product list, add a new product, change only a price, remove a test product, replace a whole product record.
Write one sentence explaining why you should not resend a POST that timed out.
activity.evidence: Your status code card and your method answers, saved as a photo or note

lessons.title: Reading JSON responses: objects, arrays and data paths
objectives: Identify JSON objects, arrays, keys and the six value types
Write a data path such as `data.authorization_url` or `hourly.temperature_2m[0]` to point at one value
Convert amounts sent in subunits, such as kobo, into naira correctly
Spot common JSON reading mistakes, such as treating a number in quotes as a number

blocks.text: Most APIs today answer in **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation). Despite the name, you do not need JavaScript to read it. JSON is plain text with a few strict rules. Once you can read it confidently, you can understand almost any API response and explain it to a client or developer.

blocks.name: organizing-data
blocks.alt: A person arranging blocks of data into order
blocks.caption: JSON organises data into named boxes inside boxes, which you can learn to open one by one.

blocks.text: The building blocks

items: An **object** is wrapped in curly brackets `{ }` and holds **key and value pairs**, such as `"email": "ada@example.com"`. Keys are always text in double quotes.
An **array** is wrapped in square brackets `[ ]` and holds a list of values in order, such as `[26.8, 27.4, 28.9]`.
A **value** can be one of six types: a string (text in double quotes), a number (no quotes), `true` or `false`, `null` (meaning empty or unknown), an object, or an array.
Commas separate items. There is no comma after the last item.

blocks.text: Because objects and arrays can contain other objects and arrays, JSON is **nested**: boxes inside boxes. Reading it is about knowing which box you are in.
Data paths: giving directions to one value

A **data path** is a short way to point at one value. You use a dot to step into an object key and square brackets with a number to pick an item from an array. Counting in arrays starts at **0**, not 1. So `[0]` is the first item, `[1]` the second, and so on. No-code tools such as Make and Zapier use the same idea when you map a field, so this skill transfers directly.

blocks.title: Walking a data path
items: Start at the whole response
Step into key: data
Step into key: authorization_url
Read the value
blocks.caption: The path `data.authorization_url` is just a set of directions, one step per dot.

blocks.text: Here is the shape of a real response from Paystack's documented Initialize Transaction endpoint (the codes are the documentation's sample values):

`{ "status": true, "message": "Authorization URL created", "data": { "authorization_url": "https://checkout.paystack.com/3ni8kdavz62431k", "access_code": "3ni8kdavz62431k", "reference": "re4lyvq3s3" } }`

The top level is an object with three keys. `status` is a boolean (`true`), `message` is a string, and `data` is another object. The path `data.reference` gives `re4lyvq3s3`, the code you would later use to check whether the payment went through. Paystack uses this same outer shape, `status`, `message`, `data`, across its API, which makes its responses predictable.

blocks.title: Worked example: pulling numbers out of arrays
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs an outdoor small chops stand at weekend events in Abuja. She asks Open-Meteo for hourly temperature and receives an `hourly` object with two arrays of equal length: `time` and `temperature_2m`. The values below are illustrative.
steps: She reads `hourly.time[0]` as `2026-10-10T12:00` and `hourly.temperature_2m[0]` as 26.8. Same position, same hour: arrays that sit side by side line up by index.
She reads the next three hours: `[1]` is 27.4, `[2]` is 28.9 and `[3]` is 30.1.
She adds the four values: 26.8 + 27.4 + 28.9 + 30.1 = 113.2.
She divides by 4 to get the average for 12:00 to 15:00: 113.2 / 4 = 28.3 degrees Celsius.
She checks `hourly_units.temperature_2m` to confirm the unit is Celsius before writing anything down.
blocks.result: Halima knows the four-hour average is 28.3 degrees Celsius and the hottest reading is at index 3 (15:00). She plans shade and cold drinks for the mid-afternoon peak.

blocks.text: Money in subunits: the kobo rule

Payment APIs usually avoid decimal points by sending money in the smallest unit. Paystack's documentation says amounts are sent in the **subunit** of the currency, so for naira that is **kobo**: multiply naira by 100 to send, divide kobo by 100 to read.

blocks.title: A costly misreading
blocks.text: If you forget the kobo rule, a 15,000 naira payment looks like 1.5 million naira in a report, or you send a request for 150 naira when you meant 15,000. Always check the documentation for the unit of every money field before you trust a total.
Common reading mistakes

items: **Quoted numbers.** `"20000"` in quotes is a string, not a number. Some APIs accept amounts as strings. A spreadsheet may treat it as text until you convert it.
**null is not zero.** `"phone": null` means no value is known. Do not report it as 0 or as an empty phone number that was confirmed.
**Off by one.** The first item in an array is `[0]`. Asking for `[1]` gives the second item.
**Missing keys.** Some keys only appear when there is data. Your process should not break if a key is absent.

blocks.text: To read long responses comfortably on a phone, paste them into a JSON viewer or use the pretty view in a tool such as Hoppscotch or Postman, which indents each level. Never paste a response that contains customer details or secret keys into a public website.

takeaways: JSON has objects in curly brackets, arrays in square brackets, and six value types
A data path uses dots for keys and [number] for array items, counting from 0
Side-by-side arrays such as time and temperature line up by index
Payment amounts are often in subunits: divide kobo by 100 to get naira
A quoted number is text, and null is not zero

activity.title: Write five data paths
steps: Request hourly temperature from Open-Meteo for your town by adding `&hourly=temperature_2m` to the URL from Lesson 1 (remove the `current` part if you like).
Write the data path to the first time value and the first temperature value.
Write down the temperatures at index 0 to 3, add them and divide by 4. Check the sum with a calculator.
Using the Paystack sample response in this lesson, write the paths to the reference and the checkout link.
Convert these kobo amounts to naira: 350000, 1200000, 99900.
activity.evidence: A note with your five data paths, your average calculation and your three conversions

quiz.q: A teammate says a request "failed with 403". What should she check first?
options: Whether the URL has a typing mistake in the host name
Whether her account or key has permission for this action
Whether the provider's servers are down
Whether the response body is valid JSON
quiz.explain: 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you are not allowed to do this, so permissions are the issue. A missing or wrong key would usually give 401.

quiz.q: In `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=9.06&longitude=7.49`, which part is the path?
quiz.explain: The path comes after the host and before the question mark. It names the endpoint on that server.

quiz.q: A POST request to create a payment times out with no response. What is the best next step?
options: Send it three times to be safe
Look up whether the first payment was created, using its reference, before retrying
Change the method to GET and resend
quiz.explain: POST is not idempotent, so resending can create a duplicate payment. Check first whether the first request succeeded.

quiz.q: A JSON field shows `"amount": 4500000` from a naira payment API that uses kobo. What is the amount in naira?
Which data path points to the third temperature in `{"hourly": {"temperature_2m": [25.1, 26.0, 27.3]}}`?
quiz.explain: Arrays count from 0, so the third item is index 2, inside the key temperature_2m, inside hourly.

quiz.q: Which header tells the server that the body you are sending is JSON?
quiz.explain: Content-Type describes the body you send. Accept describes what you want back.

modules.title: Testing, Securing and Documenting API Calls
modules.overview: You will set up free tools, send every kind of request to practice APIs, authenticate safely in test mode, and handle the failures that real integrations meet: rate limits, paged lists and webhooks. You finish with a test plan and a run sheet another person could maintain.

lessons.title: Your API toolkit: browser, Hoppscotch, Postman and curl
objectives: Choose a suitable testing tool for your device and data budget
Build GET and POST requests with query parameters, headers and a JSON body
Read the status, time and size of a response in a testing tool
Use a practice API safely, knowing that its writes are simulated

blocks.text: A browser address bar can only send GET requests, and it hides the headers. To test real APIs you need an **API client**: a tool where you pick the method, type the URL, add headers and a body, press Send, and see the full response. Here are the main options and when each one fits.

blocks.name: web-developer
blocks.alt: A developer working at a laptop with code panels
blocks.caption: An API client puts the method, URL, headers and body of a request in front of you, so nothing is hidden.

head: Tool
Runs on
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Quick GET requests to open APIs, like Open-Meteo
Cannot send POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, or set custom headers
Free, open-source API client; no install; light on data
Some APIs block requests made directly from a browser page
Desktop app or web, with a free plan
Saving collections of requests, variables, sharing with a team
The desktop app is a large download on mobile data
Exact, copyable requests; many API docs show curl examples
Text only, no buttons; easy to mistype quotes

blocks.text: You do not need all four. Many learners start with Hoppscotch on a phone, then move to Postman on a laptop when they work on larger projects. Learn to read curl even if you never type it, because most documentation, including Paystack's, shows its examples as curl commands.
Reading a curl example
Here is the shape of a documented curl request, broken down line by line:

items: `curl "https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize"`: the URL. With no other method stated and a body present, curl sends POST.
`-H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_KEY"`: `-H` adds a header. This one carries the key.
`-H "Content-Type: application/json"`: another header, saying the body is JSON.
`-d '{"email": "customer@example.com", "amount": "20000"}'`: `-d` is the body data.
`-X GET` or `-X DELETE`: when you see `-X`, it sets the method directly.

blocks.text: Once you can read this, you can copy any documented example into Hoppscotch or Postman: method in the dropdown, URL in the address box, each `-H` into the Headers tab, and the `-d` text into the Body tab as raw JSON.
The parts of a request in any tool

blocks.title: Before you press Send
items: Method chosen correctly
Full URL with path
Query parameters filled
Headers added
JSON body valid
Test environment, not live
blocks.caption: Run through these six checks on every request; most beginner errors come from skipping one.

blocks.title: Worked example: four requests to a practice API
blocks.context: For example, Chioma is training to be a no-code builder in Port Harcourt. She uses Hoppscotch on her phone and JSONPlaceholder (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com), a free fake API made for practice.
steps: GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1`. Status 200. The body is one object with `userId`, `id`, `title` and `body`.

GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?userId=1`. She adds `userId` = `1` in the Params tab and the tool writes the query string for her. The body is an array of posts that all have `userId` 1.
GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1/comments`. This is a nested route: the comments that belong to post 1.

POST `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` with header `Content-Type: application/json` and body `{"title": "Market day", "body": "Stall opens at 8", "userId": 1}`. The status is 201 Created and the response repeats her data with a new `id`.
She runs the GET for the new id and does not find her post. She checks the JSONPlaceholder guide, which says created and updated resources are not really saved: the responses are faked.
blocks.result: Chioma has practised GET with a path, GET with a query parameter, a nested route and a POST with headers and a JSON body, all without touching any real business data. She also learned to check documentation when results surprise her.

blocks.text: Reading the response panel

items: **Status**: the code and its phrase, such as 201 Created.
**Time**: how long the round trip took, in milliseconds. A sudden jump from about 300 ms to several seconds is worth noting.
**Size**: how much data came back. On costly mobile data, prefer endpoints and parameters that return only what you need.
**Headers tab**: look for `Content-Type`, and any rate limit or `Retry-After` headers.
**Body**: switch to the pretty or JSON view so nesting is indented.

blocks.text: Variables save typing and mistakes

When you repeat requests, store the parts that do not change in **variables**. In Postman, for example, you can create an environment with `base_url` set to `https://api.paystack.co` and write requests as `{{base_url}}/transaction`. Create one environment for test and one for live, and keep the secret key in the environment, not typed into each request. Switching environments then changes every request at once, which is safer than editing many URLs by hand.

blocks.title: Practice on practice APIs
blocks.text: Use open or fake APIs such as Open-Meteo and JSONPlaceholder for learning, and a provider's test mode for anything involving money or customers. Never experiment with DELETE, PUT or PATCH on a real business account.

takeaways: A browser can only test GET; an API client can send every method with headers and a body
Hoppscotch suits phones and low data; Postman suits saved collections and teams
Most documentation shows curl examples: -H is a header, -d is the body, -X sets the method
JSONPlaceholder fakes its writes, so it is safe for practising POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE
Variables and separate test and live environments reduce costly mistakes

activity.title: Run and record four practice requests
steps: Open hoppscotch.io in your browser (or Postman if you have it).
Repeat Chioma's four requests to JSONPlaceholder, using your own title and body for the POST.
For each request, write down the method, URL, status code and time taken.
Try a PATCH to `/posts/1` with body `{"title": "New title"}` and note what comes back.
Write one sentence explaining why your POST did not really create a post.
activity.evidence: A table or screenshots of five requests showing method, URL, status and time

lessons.title: From need to working call: reading docs and authenticating safely
objectives: Turn a business need into a list of endpoints, fields and permissions
Find the base URL, authentication method, limits and test mode in any API's documentation
Send an authenticated request with a Bearer token in test mode
Store and handle API keys so that a leak is unlikely and quickly contained

blocks.text: Real API work starts with a need, not with a tool. "We want to know automatically when a customer has paid" is a need. Your job is to turn it into specific API calls, test them safely, and only then connect them to a live business process.

blocks.name: secure-login
blocks.alt: A person logging in securely with a padlock on screen
blocks.caption: Most useful APIs need proof of who you are, so handling keys safely is part of every integration.

blocks.title: From need to live integration
items: State the need clearly
Read the documentation
Test in sandbox mode
Plan for errors
Go live and monitor
blocks.caption: Skipping the documentation or the sandbox step is where most failed integrations begin.

blocks.text: What to find in the documentation
Good API documentation answers the same questions every time. Before you send anything, find and write down:

items: **Base URL**: the address every endpoint starts with, for example `https://api.paystack.co`.
**Authentication**: how you prove who you are, and where the key goes (usually a header).
**Endpoints for your need**: method, path, required and optional fields, and a sample response.
**Units and formats**: money in subunits, date formats, country codes.
**Test mode or sandbox**: a separate set of keys or a separate server where nothing real happens.
**Errors and limits**: the error format, any rate limit, and how lists are split into pages.
**Change log or versioning**: how the provider announces changes.

blocks.text: How APIs check who you are

head: Method
What it looks like
Notes
rows: The most common pattern. Paystack uses this with your secret key.
`Authorization: Basic` followed by username:password encoded in base64
Base64 is easy to reverse, so it is not encryption. Only ever use it over HTTPS.
Used for "Sign in with..." and when a user grants an app access to their account.
Some APIs allow it, but URLs end up in logs and browser history, so prefer headers.

blocks.text: When credentials are missing or wrong, the server usually answers **401 Unauthorized**, and may include a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme it expects. Read the error body: it often says whether the key is missing, invalid or from the wrong mode.

It also helps to see why Basic authentication is weak. MDN's documentation uses the example username `aladdin` and password `opensesame`. Joined with a colon and encoded in base64, `aladdin:opensesame` becomes `YWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuc2VzYW1l`. Anyone who captures that header can decode it back in seconds with a free online tool. Encoding only changes how text looks; it does not lock it. That is why HTTPS, which encrypts the whole conversation, is required whenever credentials are sent, and why a Bearer key must be guarded just as carefully as a password.

blocks.title: Worked example: a test payment link with Paystack
blocks.context: For example, Ruth sells hand-made adire fabric from Abeokuta and wants a payment link for a 15,000 naira order. Her developer has given her access to the Paystack test secret key in Postman. Nothing in test mode moves real money.
steps: Need: create a payment for 15,000 naira for customer test@example.com, then confirm it was paid.
Docs: the Initialize Transaction endpoint is `POST /transaction/initialize`, needing `email` and `amount`, with amount in kobo. 15,000 x 100 = 1,500,000 kobo.

Request: method POST, URL `https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize`, headers `Authorization: Bearer` plus the test secret key and `Content-Type: application/json`, body `{"email": "test@example.com", "amount": "1500000"}`.
Response: `status` is true and `data` holds `authorization_url`, `access_code` and `reference`. She opens the authorization URL and completes the test checkout.

Check: she sends `GET /transaction/verify/` followed by the reference. She confirms `data.status` is "success", `data.currency` is "NGN" and `data.amount` is 1500000, which is 1,500,000 / 100 = 15,000 naira.
blocks.result: Ruth has proved the full flow in test mode: create, pay, verify. She also checked the amount and currency instead of trusting the word success alone. Only now will her developer switch to live keys.

blocks.title: Treat a secret key like your bank PIN
blocks.text: A secret key can act on the whole account, including money. Keep it on the server side only, never in website or app code that users download. Never send it on WhatsApp, email, or paste it into AI chat tools, screenshots or shared documents. Keep it out of code uploaded to GitHub. If a key may have leaked, generate a new one in the provider's dashboard at once, which stops the old one working, then update your systems.
Least privilege and separation

items: Use **test keys** while building and **live keys** only in the live system.
If the provider allows restricted keys or roles, give each tool only the permissions it needs, for example read-only for a reporting dashboard.
Give each project or client its own keys, so revoking one does not break the others.
Keep a private record of who has access to which key and when it was last changed.

blocks.text: Finally, confirm that your need is legal and fair to customers. Only collect the personal data the process requires, explain to customers how it will be used, and remember that API responses often contain names, phone numbers and emails that deserve the same care as paper records.

takeaways: Start from a clear need, then find base URL, auth, endpoints, units, test mode, errors and limits in the docs
Most APIs take a key in the Authorization header as a Bearer token
Basic authentication is encoded, not encrypted, so it needs HTTPS
Prove a flow end to end in test mode and verify amount and currency, not only the word success
Secret keys stay server-side; if one leaks, regenerate it immediately

activity.title: Write a one-page API fact sheet
steps: Pick an API you might use: Paystack, Open-Meteo or another with public documentation.
From its documentation, record the base URL, authentication method, two endpoints relevant to a real need, and the format of money or dates.
Note whether it has a test mode or sandbox and how you switch between test and live.
Record what it says about errors, rate limits and pagination, or write "not stated".
Add three rules for how you will store and share its keys.
activity.evidence: Your one-page fact sheet with links to the exact documentation pages used

lessons.title: Testing for failure: rate limits, pages, webhooks and the run sheet
objectives: Respond correctly to 429 and 5xx errors using Retry-After and backoff
Work out how many pages a list endpoint needs and check that totals match
Explain how a webhook is delivered, signed, acknowledged and double-checked
Write an API run sheet that lets someone else maintain the integration

blocks.text: Getting one successful response is the start of quality work, not the end. A dependable integration is one that behaves sensibly when things go wrong: too many requests, a slow server, a list that is longer than one page, or a notification that arrives twice.

blocks.name: server-error
blocks.alt: A person looking at a server showing an error
blocks.caption: Good API work plans for the error responses, not just the happy path.

blocks.text: Rate limits and retries

Most APIs limit how many requests you can make in a period of time. When you go over, the server answers **429 Too Many Requests**, and it may send a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to wait. `Retry-After: 3600` means wait 3,600 seconds, which is one hour. Respect it: hammering a server that has asked you to wait can get your access blocked.

For temporary server errors such as 502 or 503, a common pattern is **exponential backoff**: wait, retry, and double the wait each time, up to a maximum number of tries. With waits of 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds, four retries add 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 seconds of waiting before you stop and alert a person.

items: Retry automatically only when it is safe: GET, and idempotent PUT and DELETE.
Do not automatically retry a POST that creates money movements or records. Look up the result first.
Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 422: the same request will fail the same way. Fix it instead.
Log every failure with the time, endpoint, status code and the error message.

blocks.text: Lists come in pages

List endpoints usually return results in **pages**. Paystack's List Transactions endpoint, for example, takes `perPage` (records per page, default 50) and `page` (default 1), and can filter by `status` and by `from` and `to` dates. If you only read page 1, your report will quietly miss records.

blocks.title: Worked example: a month-end export that adds up
blocks.context: For example, Grace is an operations assistant for a catering business in Kaduna. She needs every successful transaction for September for the accountant. The dashboard shows 230 successful transactions for the month.
steps: She sends `GET /transaction?status=success&from=2026-09-01&to=2026-09-30&perPage=50&page=1` and checks the pagination details in the response.
Pages needed: 230 / 50 = 4.6, which rounds up to 5 pages. Pages 1 to 4 hold 50 each (200 records) and page 5 holds 230 - 200 = 30.
She requests pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn, changing only the page number.
She counts the records she collected: 50 + 50 + 50 + 50 + 30 = 230, matching the dashboard.
She converts each amount from kobo to naira (divide by 100) before giving the sheet to the accountant, and labels the column "Amount (naira)".
blocks.result: Grace's export has all 230 transactions, the count is checked against a second source, and the amounts are in the right unit. Had she stopped at page 1, 180 transactions would have been missing.

blocks.text: Webhooks: the API calls you

Checking again and again whether something has changed is called **polling**, and it wastes requests. A **webhook** reverses the direction: you give the provider a URL on your server, and the provider sends an HTTP POST to it when an event happens. Paystack, for example, sends events such as `charge.success` with a JSON body containing `event` and `data`. Its documentation recommends webhooks over polling for payment updates.

blocks.title: Handling a payment webhook safely
items: Provider POSTs the event
Check the signature
Reply 200 OK at once
Verify the transaction
Update records once
blocks.caption: Acknowledge fast, but never act on a webhook until it is proved genuine and the payment is verified.

items: **Check it is genuine.** Anyone can POST to a URL. Paystack signs each event with an HMAC SHA512 signature of the body, using your secret key, in the `x-paystack-signature` header. Your server recalculates it and rejects any mismatch. Paystack also publishes the IP addresses its webhooks come from.
**Reply quickly.** Return 200 OK immediately and do slower work afterwards; long-running handlers time out.

**Expect repeats.** If your server does not answer, Paystack retries: in live mode every 3 minutes for the first 4 tries, then hourly for 72 hours. So the same event can arrive more than once. Store each reference you have processed and skip duplicates.
**Verify before you deliver.** Call the Verify Transaction endpoint with the reference and check status, amount and currency before releasing goods.

blocks.title: Fake payment alerts
blocks.text: Scammers send fake bank alerts and screenshots. An integration that releases goods only after its own server has verified the transaction through the provider's API protects a business from this. A message, screenshot or unsigned request is never proof of payment.
The API run sheet

APIs change, keys expire and the person who built the connection moves on. A short **run sheet** lets someone else keep it working. Keep it in a shared, access-controlled folder, without any secret values written in it.

head: Section
What to record
rows: The business need in one sentence and who owns it
API name, base URL, links to the exact documentation pages used
Method, path, key fields and units for each call
Where keys are stored (not the keys), who can access them, date last rotated
Known error codes, retry rules, rate limit, page size
Test cases run, with date and result
Provider support channel and the internal person on call

takeaways: On 429, wait as long as Retry-After says; on 5xx, back off and retry only safe requests
List endpoints are paged, so count pages and check totals against a second source
A webhook is the provider calling your URL; check the signature, reply 200 fast and expect repeats
Never release goods on a screenshot or an unverified webhook
A run sheet without secrets lets someone else maintain the integration

activity.title: Write a test plan and run sheet
steps: Choose the integration from your fact sheet in the last lesson.
Write five test cases: one success, one missing field (expect 400 or 422), one wrong key (expect 401), one not found (expect 404), and one repeated event.
For a list endpoint, calculate how many pages you need for 137 records at 25 per page and how many records are on the last page.
Fill in the seven sections of the run sheet table for your integration, leaving out any secret values.
activity.evidence: Your five test cases with expected results, your page calculation and your completed run sheet

quiz.q: An API replies 429 with `Retry-After: 120`. What should the integration do?
options: Switch to a different API key and retry
Treat it as a permanent failure
quiz.explain: 429 means too many requests. Retry-After gives the number of seconds to wait, so wait 120 seconds.

quiz.q: A list endpoint returns 25 records per page and there are 137 records. How many pages must you request?
quiz.explain: 137 / 25 = 5.48, which rounds up to 6 pages. The last page holds 137 - 125 = 12 records.

quiz.q: Which of these is the safest place to keep a payment API secret key?
options: In the website's JavaScript so the checkout can use it
In a WhatsApp note to yourself
On the server, in an access-controlled environment setting
In the run sheet, so the next person can find it
quiz.explain: Secret keys must stay server-side and out of shared documents and chats. The run sheet records where keys are, not the keys.

quiz.q: A webhook says `charge.success` for 30,000 naira. What should happen before goods are released?
options: Check the signature and verify the transaction through the API, including amount and currency
Ask the customer for a screenshot
Wait 72 hours for retries to finish
quiz.explain: Anyone can POST to a URL. Check the signature, then verify the transaction with the provider's API, including amount and currency.

quiz.q: Your POST to create a customer returns 422. What is the right response?
options: Read the error message and fix the data in the request
Contact the provider because their server failed
quiz.explain: 4xx errors such as 422 mean the request itself has a problem. Retrying the same request will fail again.

quiz.q: In a curl example, what does `-H "Content-Type: application/json"` do?
options: Adds a header saying the body is JSON
Adds JSON data to the body
Saves the response to a file
quiz.explain: -H adds a header. -d adds the body, and -X sets the method.

modules.title: Consulting, Scoping and Your API Portfolio
modules.overview: You will run discovery for a real integration, turn it into a one-page spec, estimate and price it with clear scope, and build a portfolio that proves your API skills. You finish with a 90-day plan with weekly targets.

lessons.title: Discovery for an integration: questions that prevent expensive surprises
objectives: Run a discovery conversation that moves from business outcome to specific API calls
Measure the current manual effort so the value of an integration is clear
Assess a provider's documentation, sandbox, limits, costs and data handling before committing
Place possible integrations on a value and effort map and recommend where to start

blocks.text: Clients rarely ask for "an API". They describe a pain: "My staff spend the whole afternoon checking who has paid." Discovery is the structured conversation that turns that pain into a clear integration, or sometimes into the honest advice that no integration is needed. The questions below come straight from what you learned in Modules 1 and 2: each one checks a part of the request, the response, or the failure plan before money is spent.

blocks.name: questions
blocks.alt: A person surrounded by question marks
blocks.caption: Good discovery questions expose hidden costs and risks before any request is built.

blocks.text: Six areas to ask about

head: Area
Questions to ask
Why it matters
rows: What should be different when this works? Who notices first?
Defines success in business terms, not technical ones
Who does this now, how often, and how long does each one take?
Gives you a baseline to measure value against
Which exact fields are needed? Does any of it identify customers?
Shapes endpoints, privacy care and storage
Which service holds the data? Are its docs public? Is there a test mode? Any usage fees or limits?
Many projects fail on missing docs or a missing sandbox
What should happen if the API is down or slow for a day?
Forces a fallback plan, often the old manual process
Who will own the keys, the run sheet and future fixes?
Integrations need occasional care as providers change

blocks.text: Ask to **see** the current process, not only hear about it. Watching a staff member confirm one payment often reveals extra steps, such as checking two different apps or copying names into a notebook, that nobody mentions in a meeting.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery for an online foodstuff shop
blocks.context: For example, Bisi sells foodstuff online in Lagos and takes card and bank transfer payments through Paystack. Her assistant confirms each payment by hand in the dashboard before packing. Bisi asks an API consultant, Nkechi, to "connect everything".
steps: Outcome: Bisi wants orders packed within one hour of payment, and no goods released on fake alerts.
Current process: Nkechi watches the assistant work. About 40 orders a day, about 3 minutes each to confirm: 40 x 3 = 120 minutes, which is 2 hours a day.
Data: the packing list needs order number, customer name, phone, items and amount paid. Customer phone numbers are personal data, so the packing sheet will be shared only with packing staff.
Provider: Paystack's documentation is public, it has test keys, a Verify Transaction endpoint and signed webhooks such as charge.success.
Failure: if the integration is down, the assistant goes back to manual checking in the dashboard for that day.
Ownership: Bisi will own the Paystack account and keys; Nkechi will write the run sheet and offer monthly support.
blocks.result: Instead of "connect everything", Nkechi proposes one focused integration: a signed webhook plus a verify call that marks orders as paid. It targets about 2 hours of daily manual work and removes the fake alert risk, and its scope is clear enough to price.

blocks.text: Checking the provider before you commit

items: **Documentation**: is it public, current, and does it include sample requests and responses?
**Sandbox**: can you test without real money or real customers?
**Limits**: is there a published rate limit or page size, and does the client's volume fit within it?
**Cost**: does the provider charge per call or per transaction? Confirm on the provider's own pricing page and show it to the client separately from your fee.
**Support and status**: is there a status page or support channel for outages?
**Terms**: do the provider's terms allow the planned use, for example storing data or reselling access?

blocks.text: Choosing where to start

Discovery often uncovers several possible integrations. Place each one on a simple map: how much value it brings against how much effort and risk it carries. Start with high value, low effort. Leave low value, high effort ideas out of the first phase, however exciting they sound.

blocks.title: Value and effort map for integrations
items: Plan carefully: big win, big build
Do first: big win, small build
Avoid for now
Quick extras if time allows
axes: Effort and risk (high on left, low on right)
Business value (low at bottom, high at top)
blocks.caption: Recommend the top-right box first, so the client sees value early.

blocks.title: It is fine to recommend no API
blocks.text: If a client processes five payments a week, a simple daily dashboard check may cost less than building and maintaining an integration. Saying so builds trust, and that client often returns when volume grows.

End every discovery session by reading back a short summary: the outcome, the baseline numbers, the provider, the data involved, the fallback and the owner. Ask the client to correct anything wrong. This summary becomes the opening section of your specification and proposal in the next lesson.

Keep your discovery notes private and factual. Write what you saw and measured, mark guesses as guesses, and do not copy customer records into your notes. If the client shares screenshots from their dashboard, blur names, phone numbers and any keys before you save them.

takeaways: Discovery turns a vague pain into one specific, measurable integration
Measure the current manual effort, for example orders per day times minutes each
Check the provider's docs, sandbox, limits, costs, support and terms before committing
Start with high value, low effort integrations, and say so when no API is needed
Read back a summary so the client confirms outcome, data, fallback and owner

activity.title: Run a practice discovery
steps: Pick a real small business you know (a relative's shop, your church office, a friend's salon).
Ask the six areas of questions from the table and write their answers.
Measure one repeated task: how many times a day or week, and how many minutes each. Multiply to get the total time.
List two or three possible integrations and place them on the value and effort map.
Write a five-line summary and ask the owner to confirm it.
activity.evidence: Your discovery notes, time calculation, value and effort map, and the confirmed five-line summary

lessons.title: Integration specs, estimates and pricing with clear scope
objectives: Write a one-page integration specification that a developer and a client can both follow
Estimate hours task by task and add a sensible buffer for API uncertainty
Separate your fee from provider fees and ongoing maintenance in a proposal
Handle change requests without silently growing the project

blocks.text: An integration specification, or spec, is the bridge between discovery and building. It says exactly which API calls happen, when, with what data, and what counts as done. A good spec protects the client from surprises and protects you from endless extra requests.

blocks.name: business-plan
blocks.alt: A person working on a business plan document
blocks.caption: A one-page spec turns discovery notes into a buildable, priceable plan.

blocks.text: The one-page spec

items: **Goal**: one sentence from discovery, with the baseline, for example about 2 hours a day of manual payment checks.
**Trigger**: what starts the flow, such as a `charge.success` webhook.
**Calls**: each endpoint with method and path, for example `POST` to your webhook URL (incoming) and `GET /transaction/verify/:reference` (outgoing).
**Data mapping**: which response field goes where, using data paths, such as `data.amount` divided by 100 into "Amount paid (naira)".
**Rules**: signature check, duplicate check by reference, amount and currency must match the order.
**Failure plan**: alerts on repeated errors, and the manual fallback.
**Acceptance tests**: the test cases that must pass in test mode before going live.
**Out of scope**: what this project will not do.

blocks.title: Typical phases of a small integration
items: Discovery and spec
Build in test mode
Acceptance tests
Go live with monitoring
Handover and run sheet
blocks.caption: Each phase ends with something the client can see and approve.

blocks.text: Estimating honestly

API work carries uncertainty: documentation may be unclear, a field may behave differently from the sample, or the provider's test mode may differ slightly from live. Estimate each task separately, add the hours, then add a buffer. Many consultants use around 20 to 30 percent for an API they have not used before; choose your own figure from experience and state it openly.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing the payment confirmation project
blocks.context: For example, Nkechi is pricing the webhook and verify integration for Bisi's foodstuff shop. Her own rate, for illustration, is 8,000 naira per hour. Your rate will depend on your experience and market.
steps: Task estimates: spec and setup 4 hours; webhook with signature check 6 hours; verify call and order update 8 hours; testing in test mode 3 hours; run sheet and handover 3 hours.
Total: 4 + 6 + 8 + 3 + 3 = 24 hours.
Buffer of 25 percent for uncertainty: 24 x 1.25 = 30 hours.
Fee: 30 x 8,000 = 240,000 naira for the project.
Maintenance: an optional support plan of 2 hours a month, 2 x 8,000 = 16,000 naira a month, covering key rotation, small fixes and checks after provider changes.
Provider costs: Paystack's own transaction fees are listed separately as "paid by the client directly to Paystack, see their pricing page", not added to her fee.
blocks.result: Bisi receives a proposal of 240,000 naira for the project, an optional 16,000 naira monthly support plan, and a clear note that payment provider fees are separate. Every figure can be traced back to a task.

blocks.text: You can also check the price against value. If the integration saves about 2 hours of staff time a day, you can show the client how many working days it takes for the saving to cover the fee, using the client's own staff cost. Let the client supply that number; do not guess wages.
Scope and change control

head: In scope
Out of scope (quote separately)
rows: Webhook endpoint for charge.success with signature check
Refund handling and other event types
Verify call, amount and currency check, duplicate check
Sending SMS or WhatsApp messages to customers
Test mode build and five acceptance tests
Changes to the website's design or checkout page
Run sheet and one handover session
Monthly reports beyond the agreed support plan

blocks.text: When the client asks for something in the right-hand column, welcome the idea, write it down as a **change request** with its own estimate, and let the client decide. Do not add it quietly. Small unpaid additions are how fixed-price API projects become losses.

Agree payment terms that match the phases. For example, Nkechi asks for 50 percent before the build starts and 50 percent when the acceptance tests pass: 240,000 x 0.5 = 120,000 naira at each point. The support plan is billed monthly in advance and can be cancelled with notice. Write the terms in the proposal, and put each phase's approval in writing, even a short WhatsApp or email message, so there is no dispute later about what was agreed.

blocks.title: Never hold the client's keys hostage
blocks.text: The client must own the provider account and keys. Ask for access through the provider's team or role features where they exist, and remove your access at the end of the project or support plan. Your payment terms should be enforced by your contract, never by controlling their systems.

Finally, agree in writing what "done" means: the named acceptance tests pass in test mode, the client has watched one live transaction flow through correctly, and the run sheet has been handed over. When those three are true, the project is complete and support begins.

takeaways: A one-page spec lists trigger, calls, data mapping, rules, failure plan, tests and out-of-scope items
Estimate task by task, add the hours, then add a stated buffer for API uncertainty
Keep your fee, maintenance and provider fees as separate lines
New ideas become priced change requests, never silent extras
The client always owns the provider account and keys

activity.title: Spec and price one integration
steps: Use the integration you chose in your practice discovery.
Write a one-page spec with all eight headings from this lesson.
Break the work into at least five tasks with hour estimates and add them up.
Add your chosen buffer and multiply by your hourly rate. Check the arithmetic with a calculator.
Write an in-scope and out-of-scope list of at least three items each.
activity.evidence: Your one-page spec and a pricing table showing tasks, total hours, buffer, fee and separate provider costs

lessons.title: Your API portfolio: documented explorations and a 90-day plan
objectives: Document a hands-on API exploration with the request, response and your interpretation
Summarise a real API's documented capabilities accurately in your own words
Present API skills alongside no-code, automation or data work
Write a 90-day plan with weekly, checkable targets

blocks.text: Employers and clients cannot see what you understand; they can only see what you have documented. An API portfolio shows that you can read documentation, send correct requests, interpret responses and explain them clearly. Three pieces are enough to start: an exploration write-up, a documentation summary and a plan.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A portfolio website displayed on a screen
blocks.caption: A short, well-documented exploration proves more than a long list of tools.

blocks.title: Building API credibility
items: Paid client integrations
Integration spec and run sheet
Documented explorations
Core HTTP and JSON skills
blocks.caption: Each layer rests on the one below; most learners start at the base and the second layer.

blocks.text: Piece 1: the exploration write-up

Choose a public API with open documentation and no cost for learning, such as Open-Meteo or JSONPlaceholder, or a provider's test mode. Keep the write-up to one or two pages with these parts: the question you wanted answered, the endpoint and documentation link, the exact request (method, URL, headers with any key removed), the status code, a short extract of the response, your interpretation, and one thing that surprised you.

blocks.title: Worked example: an exploration write-up outline
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is a virtual assistant in Kano building her first API portfolio piece using Open-Meteo.
steps: Question: what will the maximum and minimum temperatures be in Kano over the next three days, in local time?

Request: GET `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=12.00&longitude=8.52&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&timezone=Africa/Lagos&forecast_days=3` (coordinates approximate). Status 200, Content-Type application/json.
Response extract: she pastes the `daily` object showing the `time`, `temperature_2m_max` and `temperature_2m_min` arrays, and `daily_units` showing degrees Celsius.
Interpretation: she lines up the three arrays by index and writes a three-row table of date, maximum and minimum.
Error test: she changes latitude to a text value and records the 400 response and its error message.
Surprise: she notes that without the timezone parameter, times come back in UTC, one hour behind Nigerian time.
blocks.result: Zainab's one-page write-up shows a real request, a successful response, a deliberate error, and clear interpretation. A client can read it in two minutes and see she understands APIs.

blocks.text: Piece 2: the documentation summary

Pick a business API, for example Paystack, and summarise its documented capabilities in your own words, in about 300 words. Cover the base URL, how authentication works, three or four main endpoints and what each does, units and formats, test mode, and how webhooks are signed. Link to each documentation page you used, and write only what the documentation actually says. If you are unsure of something, say "not covered in the pages I read" instead of guessing.

A good summary reads like a briefing for a busy manager. Start with one sentence on what the API is for, then a short list of capabilities, then the safety points: test mode, key handling and webhook signatures. End with two or three questions you would ask the provider before using it for a real client. This shows judgement, not just reading.
Piece 3: connecting API skill to your other work

items: **No-code builders**: show how a custom API call extended a tool beyond its built-in connections.
**Automation**: show the webhook or HTTP step in a workflow and the data mapping you designed.
**Data and reporting**: show a paged export that you checked against a second source.
**Project coordination**: show a spec, test plan and run sheet you wrote, even for a practice project.

blocks.title: Clean before you publish
blocks.text: Before sharing any screenshot or write-up, remove keys, tokens, signatures, customer names, emails, phone numbers and real transaction references. Use test mode data or fake data from practice APIs. One leaked key in a portfolio can undo the trust it was meant to build.
Your 90-day plan

head: Weeks
Focus
Checkable target
rows: 20 requests logged across Open-Meteo and JSONPlaceholder
One published write-up with an error test
Create and verify one test payment; documentation summary written
Full spec and run sheet for a practice integration
One automation or no-code project using a custom API call
Two discovery conversations and one proposal sent or one internal improvement delivered

blocks.text: Review the plan every two weeks. If a target slips, shrink it rather than drop it. API documentation and tools change, so date every write-up and recheck links before sharing your portfolio with a new client.

Keep the whole portfolio light. Many clients will open it on a phone with limited data, so prefer a single shared folder or a simple web page with short PDFs and compressed screenshots. Give each piece a one-line headline that says what it proves, for example "Read a weather API, handled a 400 error, converted UTC to Nigerian time". Put your strongest piece first, and add new pieces as your 90-day plan moves forward.

takeaways: Three pieces make a starting portfolio: an exploration write-up, a documentation summary and a plan
Show the request, the status, a response extract, your interpretation and a deliberate error
Write only what the documentation says and link to each page
Remove every key, token and customer detail before publishing
A 90-day plan needs weekly, checkable targets and regular review

activity.title: Draft your first portfolio piece
steps: Choose a question you can answer with Open-Meteo or JSONPlaceholder.
Send the request in Hoppscotch or Postman and save the URL, status and a response extract.
Send one deliberate bad request and record the error status and message.
Write your interpretation in five sentences or a small table.
Draft your 90-day plan using the table in this lesson, changing targets to fit your goals.
activity.evidence: Your one-page exploration write-up and your 90-day plan

quiz.q: A client says, "Connect everything to the payment app." What is the best first step?
options: Start building webhooks for every event type
Ask what should be different when it works and measure the current manual process
Send a price for a full integration
Ask for the live secret key
quiz.explain: Discovery starts with the outcome and a measured baseline, so the integration can be focused and priced.

quiz.q: A shop handles 25 orders a day and confirming each takes 4 minutes. How much time does manual confirmation take each day?
quiz.explain: 25 x 4 = 100 minutes, which is 1 hour 40 minutes a day.

quiz.q: Task estimates add up to 32 hours and you add a 25 percent buffer. What is the total?
During the build, the client asks you to also send WhatsApp messages to customers. This was not in the spec. What should you do?
options: Add it quietly to keep the client happy
Record it as a change request with its own estimate and let the client decide
Remove a test case to make time for it
quiz.explain: Out-of-scope ideas become priced change requests, so the client chooses with full information.

quiz.q: Which item should NOT appear in a published portfolio write-up?
options: The endpoint URL and documentation link
A test secret key used in the request
quiz.explain: Never publish keys, even test keys, or customer details. Remove them before sharing.

quiz.q: Who should own the payment provider account and API keys after an integration project?
options: The consultant, until the final invoice is paid
The developer who wrote the code
quiz.explain: The client owns the account and keys. Consultants get access through roles and remove it when work ends.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement best describes an API?
options: A website design for mobile phones
A published set of rules that lets one program request data or actions from another
A database that stores customer records
A type of mobile money account
finalQuiz.explain: An API defines how a client may ask a server for data or actions and what the answer will look like.
The host is the server's name, between the scheme and the path.

finalQuiz.q: Which method should you use to change only the phone number on an existing customer record?
finalQuiz.explain: PATCH applies a partial change. PUT would replace the whole record.

finalQuiz.q: A request returns 401 Unauthorized. What is the most likely cause?
options: The key is missing or invalid
finalQuiz.explain: 401 means the server did not receive valid proof of identity. 503 is overload, 301 is a moved address, 429 is too many requests.

finalQuiz.q: A response shows `"amount": 750000` from a naira API that uses kobo. What is the amount?

options: The last maximum temperature in the list
The first maximum temperature in the daily object
The unit of the maximum temperature
finalQuiz.explain: Arrays count from 0, so [0] is the first item of the temperature_2m_max array inside daily.

finalQuiz.q: Why is JSONPlaceholder a good place to practise POST, PUT and DELETE?
options: It charges very little per request
Its writes are faked, so no real data is changed
It requires a secret key for safety
finalQuiz.explain: Its guide states that created, updated and deleted resources are not really changed on the server; the responses are simulated.

finalQuiz.q: A server replies 503 to a GET request. What is a sensible automatic response?
options: Retry with growing waits, such as 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds, then alert a person
Delete the record and try again
finalQuiz.explain: 503 is a temporary server problem. Exponential backoff with a limit is sensible for safe requests such as GET.

finalQuiz.q: There are 95 records and the page size is 20. How many records are on the last page?
finalQuiz.explain: 95 / 20 = 4.75, so 5 pages are needed. Four full pages hold 80, leaving 95 - 80 = 15 on the last page.

finalQuiz.q: What is the main purpose of checking the `x-paystack-signature` header on a webhook?
options: To find the customer's phone number
To prove the event really came from Paystack and was not altered
To decide how long to wait before retrying
finalQuiz.explain: Paystack signs each event body with HMAC SHA512 using your secret key. Recalculating it proves the event is genuine.

finalQuiz.q: A client's integration estimate is 20 hours plus a 30 percent buffer, at an illustrative rate of 10,000 naira per hour. What is the fee?
Which should a run sheet contain?
options: The live secret key so others can find it
Where keys are stored, who can access them and when they were last rotated
finalQuiz.explain: A run sheet documents where credentials live and who controls them, never the secret values themselves.

capstone.title: API Exploration and Documentation Project
capstone.brief: Produce a three-part portfolio pack: a documented hands-on exploration of a real public API showing your request and interpreted response, a summary in your own words of a real business API's documented capabilities, and a 90-day plan for applying API skills alongside your other technical work.
steps: Choose a question you can answer with a free public API such as Open-Meteo, and read the relevant documentation page.
Send the request in Hoppscotch or Postman, record the method, URL, headers (with any key removed), status and a response extract.
Send one deliberate bad request, record the error status and message, and explain what it means.
Interpret the response in a short table or paragraph, using data paths to show where each value came from.
Write a 300-word summary of a business API such as Paystack, linking every documentation page you used.
Write your 90-day plan with fortnightly, checkable targets and review dates.
Clean every file of keys, tokens and personal data, then share the pack with a peer for feedback.
evidence: Exploration write-up with request, status, response extract, interpretation and an error test
Documentation summary with links to each page used
Confirmation that no keys or personal data appear in any file
Peer feedback note and the changes you made
